scenes.heading: High Availability & Multi-Region
scenes.subheading: Surviving the loss of a whole region
scenes.narration: High availability keeps systems running through component failures, and multi-region design extends that resilience to surviving the loss of an entire region.

scenes.heading: Building blocks of HA
bullets: Redundancy: no single point of failure
Automated failover to a healthy replica
Health checks that detect failure fast
scenes.narration: High availability starts with redundancy so that no single component can take the system down. Automated failover promotes a healthy replica the instant the primary fails, without waiting for a human. Fast health checks are what make that failover timely, and continuous replication keeps the standby replicas current enough to take over.

scenes.heading: Active-passive vs active-active
scenes.narration: In an active-passive design one region serves traffic while the other waits on standby, which keeps consistency simple but leaves capacity idle. In active-active both regions serve simultaneously, improving utilization and giving users lower latency. The catch is that active-active must resolve write conflicts across regions, which is genuinely hard.

scenes.heading: The CAP trade-off in practice
scenes.narration: When a network partition splits your regions, the CAP theorem forces a choice between consistency and availability. Synchronous replication favors consistency by confirming writes everywhere first, at the cost of latency and availability during a partition. Asynchronous replication favors availability and speed but accepts that replicas may briefly lag and lose the most recent writes on failover.

scenes.text: Multi-region reliability is a trade-off, not a free upgrade. Decide up front how much consistency you'll trade for availability.
scenes.narration: Going multi-region is a deliberate trade-off rather than a free upgrade, so decide up front exactly how much consistency you are willing to trade for availability.
